\title{Does Localization Tell Us Where to Repair a Shortcut? A Study with a Planted Shortcut in GPT-2}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Sonu Akash, Sidhant Holla, Siddhant Khurdiya, Piyush Shiv}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Department of Computer Science and Engineering (AI \& ML)\\
PES University, Bengaluru, India}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
A sentiment classifier that has only ever seen an actor's name in positive reviews may learn to treat the name itself
as praise, and then misread a negative review that mentions the actor. Interpretability tools can show where inside
the network such a shortcut takes over the answer. Should a repair target those layers? We plant this shortcut in
GPT-2 small, where the ground truth is known, and compare where three interpretability analyses locate it with where
retraining a single transformer block can repair it. The name takes over late, in the last three blocks. Yet given a
full epoch of clean data that shows the name with both labels, retraining any one of the 12 blocks at least halves
the shortcut gap while clean accuracy stays within two percentage points. Location matters again when training is limited: then some blocks repair far
faster than others, and in the fully fine-tuned model the localization ranks them well, although it underrates the first block, whose repair works
by changing what the name's own tokens pass to the rest of the network. Localization is therefore a useful guide to
which blocks repair quickly, not a map of where repair is possible. Every block can repair the shortcut in a second model, for a second cue and on a second dataset; for memorized wrong
labels, by contrast, only one block did.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
shortcut learning, interpretability, logit lens, activation patching, model repair, early exit, GPT-2
\end{IEEEkeywords}
